profile.summary: Caduceus is a family of DNA language models for long human genomic sequences. It reads DNA one base at a time, looking both upstream and downstream, and is built so that a sequence and its reverse complement are treated consistently. The pretrained models output masked-base predictions and per-base embeddings that can be fine-tuned or used as features, for example for variant effect prediction.
profile.summary_source_locator: arXiv abstract; model card: Model Details; README: eQTL SNP Variant Effect Prediction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Caduceus builds on the long-range Mamba block. The authors extend it to a BiMamba component that reads a sequence in both directions, and to a MambaDNA block that is also reverse-complement (RC) equivariant. The published checkpoints have hidden dimension 256 and 16 MambaDNA layers and were pretrained as masked language models on the human reference genome. In the RC-equivariant Caduceus-PS model the hidden state is twice the width of a non-equivariant model, and the card says to run a downstream model on the hidden state and its reverse complement, or average them, to get RC-invariant outputs.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The README lists two pretrained checkpoints on Hugging Face. Caduceus-Ph was trained with reverse-complement data augmentation. Caduceus-PS is RC equivariant by design and needs no augmentation. Both were trained on sequences of length 131k with model size 256 and 16 layers, for 50k steps at batch size 8. A result should name the checkpoint (Ph or PS) and its Hugging Face revision; this page read PS at revision d89eeb85 and Ph at revision b0477522. The repository also holds the training code used to reproduce the paper's pretraining and fine-tuning experiments.

profile.summary: HyenaDNA is a family of DNA language models that read very long stretches of genome one base at a time, up to 1 million bases in the largest model. It was pretrained on the human reference genome by predicting the next base, and it outputs per-base embeddings that can be fine-tuned for tasks such as finding regulatory elements or classifying species.
profile.summary_source_locator: README: Intro; model card: Model & Training Overview; arXiv abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: HyenaDNA replaces attention with a stack of Hyena operators, which use input projections, implicit long convolutions and gating and scale sub-quadratically with sequence length. Each layer has a global receptive field. A single-character tokenizer with a vocabulary of the 4 nucleotides plus special tokens keeps single-base resolution. The model is causal: it is pretrained by next-nucleotide prediction on the human reference genome (HG38), and the inference script pads on the left for that reason.

Each exists as a weights-only repository for the original GitHub code and as a transformers-compatible copy with an -hf suffix; the model card says the two give identical outputs. A result should name the checkpoint, which interface was used, and the revision; this page read LongSafari/hyenadna-large-1m-seqlen-hf at revision 0a629abf. A Docker image with the exact Nucleotide Transformer benchmark settings from the paper is also provided.

profile.summary: GENA-LM is a family of transformer DNA language models for reading long genomic sequences, up to 36,000 base pairs in its sparse-attention versions. It takes DNA split into variable-length tokens and returns sequence representations that are fine-tuned for tasks such as promoter, splice site, enhancer and chromatin profile prediction. Most models were trained on the human T2T genome, and species-specific and multispecies models also exist.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Materials and methods (Sequence tokenization); README_previous_generation.md: Pre-trained models, Downstream tasks

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GENA-LM models are BERT-style transformer encoders trained as masked language models. DNA is first split by a Byte-Pair Encoding tokenizer with a dictionary of 32 000 tokens, so one token covers several bases; the paper reports a median token length of 9 bp. BERT models use pre-layer normalisation. Three models reach 4096 tokens (about 36,000 bp): two use DeepSpeed sparse attention with rotary position embeddings, and bigbird-base-t2t uses the Hugging Face BigBird implementation. The paper also describes fine-tuning with a recurrent memory mechanism to process even longer segments.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Sequence tokenization, Abstract; README_previous_generation.md: Pre-trained models

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The repository table lists eight pretrained checkpoints: five BERT models of 512 tokens (4500 bp) and three BigBird-style models of 4096 tokens (36000 bp). They differ in depth (12 or 24 layers), in the data used for the tokenizer and for training (T2T only, T2T with 1000 Genomes SNPs, or with multispecies data), and in which chromosomes were held out. The paper also names yeast, fly and Arabidopsis models. Fine-tuned checkpoints for promoters and splice sites are kept as branches of the Hugging Face repositories. A result should name the checkpoint, the branch if any, and the Hugging Face revision; this page read gena-lm-bert-base-t2t at revision 4f1352bd. The developers have since released a successor family, modernGENA, in the same repository.

profile.summary: Nucleotide Transformer v3 (NTv3) is a family of DNA models from InstaDeep that read up to about 1 million bases at single-base resolution, across many species. Pre-trained checkpoints learn from unlabelled genomes by predicting masked bases and give embeddings. Post-trained checkpoints are further trained to predict functional genomics tracks (such as chromatin accessibility, histone marks and transcription factor binding) and genome annotations, given the species.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: NTv3 is a U-Net. A convolutional tower shortens the single-base token sequence by 2 to the power of the number of downsampling blocks (128 for the main models, which have 7), a transformer processes the compressed sequence with self-attention, and a deconvolutional tower with skip connections restores single-base resolution. Pre-training uses masked language modelling on 9 trillion base pairs from OpenGenome2, with a length curriculum up to 1 Mb. Post-training adds supervised learning on about 16,000 functional tracks and annotation labels from 24 species, with adaptive layer norms for species conditioning. Post-trained track and annotation outputs cover the middle 37.5% of the input.

profile.summary: Evo is a 7-billion-parameter DNA language model trained on prokaryotic whole genomes. It reads DNA one base at a time, with a context of 8,192 or 131,072 bases depending on the checkpoint, and predicts the next base. The developers use it to score how likely a sequence is and to generate new DNA, from single genes and CRISPR-Cas systems up to genome-scale sequences.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Evo uses the StripedHyena architecture, a hybrid of multi-head attention and gated convolutions arranged in Hyena blocks. Hyena layers do most of the sequence processing and attention layers add targeted pattern recall, which gives near-linear scaling of compute and memory with context length. Tokens are single nucleotides (byte-level). The model is autoregressive: it outputs logits over the vocabulary at each position, which are used to sample new sequence or to score the log-likelihood of an existing one. Generation can run in a recurrent mode; the model card reports more than 500k bases generated on a single 80GB GPU.

profile.summary: LucaOne is a biological foundation model that reads nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) and protein sequences with one shared model. Given a sequence and its type, it returns an embedding: a matrix with one vector per residue or a single vector for the whole sequence. These embeddings are used as inputs to downstream models for sequence-level or residue-level classification and regression.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: LucaOne (also called LucaGPLM) is a transformer encoder over a joint vocabulary of nucleotides and amino acids. The published checkpoint has a masked language model head, which the developers describe as for pre-training and sequence recovery; the full set of pretraining tasks is described in the paper, which was not read. The published default checkpoint has 20 layers, hidden size 2560, 40 attention heads and a 39-token vocabulary, with no absolute position embeddings. Each input is marked as gene (DNA or RNA) or prot. The output is the last hidden layer: per-token vectors including [CLS] and [SEP], which can be pooled to one vector by mean, [CLS] or trainable attention pooling. Long sequences are split into overlapping fragments and the embeddings merged.

steps.title: Embed a nucleotide sequence
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
import lucaone
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel, TrainingArguments, Trainer

# model_id
model_id = "LucaGroup/LucaOne-default-step36M"

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    trust_remote_code=True,
    force_download=True
)

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(
    model_id,
    task_level="token_level",
    task_type="embedding",
    trust_remote_code=True,
    force_download=True
)

# device
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
model.to(device)
model.eval()

# nucleotide sequence
nucleotide_sequence = "ATGCGTACGTTAGC"
nucleotide_inputs = tokenizer(
    nucleotide_sequence,
    # note: gene sequence(for DNA or RNA), seq_type must be 'gene'
    seq_type="gene",
    return_tensors="pt",
    add_special_tokens=True
)
new_nucleotide_inputs = {}
for item in nucleotide_inputs.items():
    new_nucleotide_inputs[item[0]] = item[1].to(device)
nucleotide_inputs = new_nucleotide_inputs

with torch.no_grad():
    nucleotide_outputs = model(**nucleotide_inputs)
    # last hidden matrix as embedding matrix: [batch_size, seq_len + 2, hidden_size]
    nucleotide_last_hidden = nucleotide_outputs.last_hidden_state
    # mean pooling
    mean_nucleotide_embedding = nucleotide_last_hidden[:, 1:-1, :].mean(dim=1)
print(f"Nucleotide Embedding Shape: {nucleotide_last_hidden.shape}")
print(mean_nucleotide_embedding)
PY

profile.summary: GPN-Star is a DNA language model that predicts how strongly each position of a genome is constrained by evolution, and so how damaging a single-nucleotide variant there is likely to be. It reads a window of a whole-genome alignment of many species with their species tree, predicts masked nucleotides of the target genome, and scores a variant by how much less likely the alternate allele is than the reference. Human models exist at vertebrate, mammal and primate timescales, and further models cover five model organisms.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GPN-Star is an encoder-only Transformer trained to predict masked nucleotides. Each input is a window of a whole-genome alignment and its species tree. The alignment is split into target sequences and source sequences. Source species that are closely related are pooled into clade-level representations. Each encoder block has self-attention along the target sequence, a phylogeny-informed cross-attention module that reads the source sequences weighted by evolutionary distances from the species tree, and a feed-forward network. The published vertebrate human checkpoint has 16 layers, hidden size 1024 and 16 attention heads.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Main, Fig. 1 legend and model description; config.json

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: Eight checkpoints are published. Three are human (hg38) models of 200M parameters each, trained on a 100-way vertebrate, a 447-way mammalian and a 243-way primate alignment; the paper calls them GPN-Star (V), (M) and (P). Five are for model organisms: mouse and chicken (85M parameters), fly (85M), worm and arabidopsis (25M). Each checkpoint needs the alignment it was trained on, with matching assembly, species set, species order and evolutionary scale. Genome-wide scores are published, so many uses need no inference. A result should name the checkpoint and its Hugging Face revision, whether published scores or new inference were used, and the window size.

profile.summary: GENERator is a family of generative DNA language models: it reads a DNA sequence and predicts what comes next, so it can both generate new sequence and produce embeddings for downstream tasks. The models are Transformer decoders that read DNA in 6-letter chunks (6-mers), with a context of up to 98k base pairs. The first release was trained on 386 billion nucleotides of eukaryotic DNA; a second release (GENERator-v2) adds eukaryote and prokaryote models.

GENERator-v2 adds a training objective that recovers single-nucleotide likelihoods from k-mer tokens, and pretraining data concentrated on gene-centric and regulatory regions.

python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    "GenerTeam/GENERator-eukaryote-1.2b-base",
    attn_implementation="flash_attention_2",
    trust_remote_code=True,
    dtype=torch.bfloat16,
).cuda().eval()

    "GenerTeam/GENERator-eukaryote-1.2b-base",
    trust_remote_code=True,
)

    "ATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCGATCG",
    "ACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGTACGT"
]

inputs = tokenizer(
    processed_sequences,
    add_special_tokens=False,
    return_tensors="pt",
    padding=True,
    padding_side="left",
).to("cuda")

    outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=32, do_sample=False)

decoded_sequences = tokenizer.batch_decode(outputs, skip_special_tokens=True)
print(decoded_sequences)
PY

profile.summary: Borzoi is a neural network that predicts RNA-seq coverage, the read depth along genes in different cell types and tissues, directly from DNA sequence. It takes a 524 kb stretch of human or mouse genome and outputs predicted coverage for thousands of experiments in 32 bp bins. Comparing predictions for the reference and the variant sequence gives scores for a variant's effect on gene expression, splicing and polyadenylation.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract; README.md: introduction

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Borzoi is a supervised model, not a language model: it is trained to reproduce measured coverage tracks. It uses the core Enformer architecture, a tower of convolution and pooling blocks followed by self-attention blocks at 128 bp resolution, then a U-net that upsamples back to 32 bp resolution. The training targets are RNA-seq coverage from ENCODE and GTEx plus the Enformer training data (CAGE, DNase-seq, ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq). Variant effects are computed from the difference between predicted coverage for the reference and the alternate sequence, summarised by statistics such as logSED for gene expression, COVR for polyadenylation and nDi for splicing.

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: The published model is four replicates trained with identical data splits, each distributed as a human and a mouse .h5 weight file. The authors report that an ensemble of the four replicates generally performed better than any single replicate. A separate collection of smaller Mini Borzoi models, trained on subsets of data types or with architecture changes, is also published. The repository has legacy and latest data transforms; the legacy transforms match the manuscript. A result should say which replicates were used, whether they were averaged, and which transform was applied.

profile.summary: DeepVariant is a germline variant caller: it finds SNPs and small indels in a person's sequencing reads. It takes reads aligned to a reference genome, turns the reads around each candidate site into a pileup image, classifies that image with a convolutional neural network, and writes the calls to a VCF or gVCF file. Trained models are provided for short-read, long-read and other sequencing technologies, all trained on human data.
profile.summary_source_locator: README.md: introduction and notes; paper title

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: DeepVariant runs as three programs. make_examples reads the aligned reads and the reference and writes a multi-channel tensor for each candidate site. All models use six base channels (read base, base quality, mapping quality, strand, whether the read supports the allele, and whether the base matches the reference); Illumina models add an insert size channel and PacBio and ONT models add a haplotype channel. call_variants classifies each tensor with a convolutional network and is the only step that uses a GPU. The usage guide's section on changes since the 2016 precisionFDA challenge says the model moved to the Inception-v3 architecture; the sources read do not state the architecture of the v1.10 models. postprocess_variants sorts the results, combines multi-allelic records and writes a VCF, and optionally a gVCF. Genotypes are limited to hom-ref, het and hom-alt.

profile.summary: 3UTRBERT is an RNA language model for 3' untranslated regions (3'UTRs), the stretch of an mRNA after the coding sequence that carries many regulatory signals. It is a BERT model pre-trained on human 3'UTR sequences, read as overlapping k-mer tokens, and then fine-tuned to predict RNA-binding protein sites, m6A modification sites and where an mRNA sits in the cell. Its attention scores can be used to highlight regions with likely regulatory function.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: 3UTRBERT is the encoder part of a Transformer: token embeddings of dimension 768 plus positional embeddings pass through twelve stacked Transformer layers, each with multi-head self-attention and a feed-forward layer. Sequences are split into overlapping k-mer tokens. It was pre-trained as a masked language model: 15% of the k-mers are masked, in contiguous spans of k tokens so that a masked k-mer cannot be read off its neighbours, and the model learns to restore them; next sentence prediction was dropped. For downstream use, the model is either fine-tuned end to end on short labelled sequences, or frozen and used to extract embeddings for longer sequences.

profile.summary: Enformer is a neural network that predicts gene expression and other genomic signals directly from DNA sequence. It reads about 200 kb of sequence and predicts 5,313 human (or 1,643 mouse) tracks, such as CAGE, DNase-seq, ATAC-seq and ChIP-seq signal, in 128 bp bins across the central 114,688 bp. Comparing predictions for reference and alternate sequences gives variant effect scores, and precomputed scores are published for common 1000 Genomes variants.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract and Methods, Model architecture; README.md: Pre-computed variant effect predictions

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Enformer is a supervised model trained to reproduce measured genomic tracks. It has three parts: seven convolutional blocks with pooling that reduce 196,608 bp to 1,536 positions of 128 bp each, eleven transformer blocks that let distant positions exchange information, and a cropping layer followed by pointwise convolutions into separate human and mouse output heads. The transformer layers use relative positional basis functions and give a receptive field that reaches elements up to 100 kb away. It was trained jointly on human and mouse data from the Basenji2 dataset, with the input extended to 196,608 bp.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Methods, Model architecture and Training; Results

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: One pre-trained model is published, at https://tfhub.dev/deepmind/enformer/1, with code to load its weights into the Sonnet Enformer module for fine-tuning. The README's inference example passes 393,216 bp, of which the model uses only the central 196,608 bp. Precomputed SAD and SAR variant scores on hg19 and their top 20 principal components are published for frequent 1000 Genomes variants. The paper also describes fine-tuning the model on human data. A result should state the model URL and version, whether published scores were used, and the genome build.

profile.summary: DNAGPT is a GPT-style DNA language model from Tencent AI Lab and collaborators. It reads a DNA sequence, split into 6-letter words, and can also take numbers as input; it can generate new DNA sequence, classify a sequence or predict a numerical value such as mRNA expression level. Pre-training adds two side tasks, predicting whether a sequence was reversed and predicting its GC content, to the usual next-token prediction.

sections.body: DNAGPT is a decoder-only Transformer: the 0.1B model has 12 blocks of unidirectional attention, 12 heads each and a hidden size of 768. The DNA sequence is cut into non-overlapping k-mers, and numbers are encoded as separate number tokens; each token type has its own embedding layer and output head. Pre-training combines three tasks: next-token prediction, GC-content prediction for a random segment, and prediction of whether the sequence order was flipped. Reversing sequences lets the left-to-right model use context from both directions. For a downstream task the needed heads are kept and the model is fine-tuned.

profile.summary: JanusDNA is a DNA language model that reads sequence one nucleotide at a time and is designed for long inputs. It is pre-trained on the human reference genome so that each position is predicted from the sequence on both sides of it, and its learned representations are then fine-tuned for tasks such as regulatory element classification and eQTL prediction. The models are small: the README lists sizes of 1.980M to 2.009M and 7.662M parameters.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The input sequence is encoded by two independent stacks, one reading left to right and one right to left. Each stack has 8 layers, each with a Mamba block and a feed-forward block, and half of the feed-forward blocks are replaced by mixture-of-experts blocks with 16 experts. A final fusion layer, a FlexAttention layer with 4 heads, joins the two directions with an attention mask that lets the prediction for a position see the left context from the forward pass and the right context from the backward pass, but not the position itself. This lets every token contribute to the loss, as in autoregressive training, while the model still learns from both sides, as in masked training. One variant also replaces the Mamba block in the fifth layer with a causal attention layer (mid-attention). A later update adds two MLP layers after the fusion layer.

The 32 and 72 widths come with and without mid-attention. The weights dataset on Harvard Dataverse (version 2) holds five original checkpoints with their configuration files and five later checkpoints with the final MLP layers (JanusDNA_mlp), which the README calls the latest. profile.summary: LAMAR is an RNA language model from the Shanghai Institute of Nutrition and Health (CAS) for studying how RNA processing is regulated. It reads an RNA sequence one nucleotide at a time and returns an embedding for each nucleotide; fine-tuned versions predict splice sites, translation efficiency from 5' UTRs, mRNA degradation from 3' UTRs and internal ribosome entry sites (IRES). steps.title: Compute embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
from LAMAR.modeling_nucESM2 import EsmModel
from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoTokenizer
from safetensors.torch import load_file, load_model
import torch


seq = "ATACGATGCTAGCTAGTGACTAGCTGATCGTAGCTG"
model_max_length = 1026
device = torch.device("cuda:0")
# instance tokenizer and config
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("tokenizer/single_nucleotide/", model_max_length=model_max_length)
config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(
    "config/config_150M.json", vocab_size=len(tokenizer), pad_token_id=tokenizer.pad_token_id,
    mask_token_id=tokenizer.mask_token_id, token_dropout=False, positional_embedding_type='rotary',
    hidden_size=768, intermediate_size=3072, num_attention_heads=12, num_hidden_layers=12
)
# intance the model and load pretrained weights
model = EsmModel(config)
weights = load_file('pretrain/saving_model/mammalian80D_4096len1mer1sw_80M/checkpoint-250000/model.safetensors')
weights_dict = {}
for k, v in weights.items():
    new_k = k.replace('esm.', '') if 'esm' in k else k
    weights_dict[new_k] = v
model.load_state_dict(weights_dict, strict=False)
model = model.to(device)
# Compute embeddings
model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    inputs = tokenizer(seq, return_tensors="pt")
    input_ids = inputs['input_ids'].to(device)
    attention_mask = inputs['attention_mask'].to(device)
    outputs = model(
        input_ids=input_ids,
        attention_mask=attention_mask
    )
    embedding = outputs.last_hidden_state[0, 1 : -1, :]
print(embedding.shape)
PY

profile.summary: Genos is a family of DNA language models for the human genome from the Genos Team in Hangzhou, China (GitHub and Hugging Face organisation BGI-HangzhouAI). It reads DNA one base at a time, with inputs of up to about one million bases, and is trained to predict the next base. Its internal representations (embeddings) are used for tasks such as classifying genomic elements, predicting variant effects and, after fine-tuning, predicting RNA-seq coverage from DNA sequence.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Genos is a decoder-style Transformer with a mixture-of-experts feed-forward layer. Each base (A, T, C, G or N) is one token. Every layer has grouped-query attention, with 16 heads sharing 8 key-value groups, and rotary position embeddings for long contexts; a router sends each token to 2 of 8 expert networks. A final linear layer gives the probability of the next base, which is the training objective. Pre-training mixed sequence lengths of 8,192, 32,768, 131,072 and 1,024,000 bp. For downstream use the paper names three modes: embedding extraction, sequence generation and fine-tuning.

steps.title: Extract embeddings
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel, AutoTokenizer

# Specify model path
model_path = "/path/to/your/local/Genos-1.2B" # Replace with local model path

# Load tokenizer and model
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_path)

# Load locally downloaded Genos weights
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained(model_path,
                                  output_hidden_states=True,
                                  torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
                                  trust_remote_code=True,
                                  attn_implementation="flash_attention_2" # Use flash_attention
  )
model.cuda() # Load model to GPU
model.eval() # Switch model to inference mode

import random

# Randomly select a specific number of bases
bases = ['A', 'T', 'G', 'C']
seqs = random.choices(bases, k=8192)
# Generate input base sequence
text = ''.join(seqs)

# Encode text
inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt")

# Load data to GPU
inputs = {k: v.cuda() for k, v in inputs.items()}

# Model inference
with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model(**inputs)

# Get hidden states from all layers
hidden_states = outputs.hidden_states  # Tuple containing hidden states from each layer

# Iterate through embeddings from each layer and display key information
for i, layer_embedding in enumerate(hidden_states):
    print(f"Layer {i} embedding ({layer_embedding.shape}): {layer_embedding[0, 0, :10]}")
    print("-" * 50)
PY

profile.summary: RNABERT is a small RNA language model from Keio University that turns each base of a non-coding RNA sequence into a numerical vector (an embedding) that reflects its sequence context and secondary structure. It reads RNA sequences in FASTA format and outputs per-base embeddings, which the authors use to align RNAs by structure and to cluster them into RNA families.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Abstract, Introduction; README.md: Data processing, Earn embeddings

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: Each base gets a 120-dimensional token embedding plus a position embedding, and the sum passes through six Transformer layers. The output is a context-sensitive embedding for every base. Training alternates two tasks. In masked language modelling (MLM), some bases are hidden and predicted from the rest. In structural alignment learning (SAL), pairs of sequences from Rfam seed alignments are aligned using their embeddings, so that bases aligned in the reference alignment get similar embeddings. A structural alignment of two RNAs is then computed from the embeddings with the Needleman-Wunsch algorithm.

The README says this model was trained on the full Rfam 14.3 dataset (about 400 nucleotides), while the paper describes MLM pre-training on 76 237 human small ncRNAs from RNAcentral and SAL training on Rfam alignments (TrainSet-A or TrainSet-B). profile.summary: BPNet is a convolutional neural network that predicts transcription-factor binding from DNA sequence at single-base resolution. It reads a stretch of genomic sequence and predicts the strand-specific read profile and the total read count of a ChIP-nexus or ChIP-seq experiment over that region. It is not a pretrained model: users train a new BPNet on their own experiment, then interpret it to find the sequence motifs that drive binding.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper abstract; README.md opening paragraph

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: In the paper, the body of the network is a first convolutional layer of 64 filters of width 25 bp, followed by 9 dilated convolutional layers of 64 filters of width 3, with the dilation rate doubling at every layer and no pooling, so base resolution is kept. Two output heads per transcription factor sit on top: a deconvolutional layer that predicts the probability of a read at each position on each strand (profile shape), and a global average pooling layer with a fully connected layer that predicts the total read count. The loss is a multinomial negative log-likelihood for profile shape plus a mean squared error on log total counts. A control track is given as an extra input so that experimental bias is regressed out. After training, contribution scores and TF-MoDISco are used to extract motifs.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Results, 'BPNet predicts TF binding profiles from sequence'; Methods, BPNet architecture and loss function

sections.title: Versions and reproducibility
sections.body: There are two generations of the code in the same repository. The original package that accompanied the paper is kept at the v0-final tag; it uses a `bpnet train` command, a dataspec.yml file and Python 3.6 with TensorFlow 1. The current master branch is described by its authors as the improved version and the one to use; it has separate `bpnet-train`, `bpnet-predict` and `bpnet-shap` commands, Python 3.7, and an example configuration with a 2114 bp input, a 1000 bp output profile, a first filter of width 21 and 8 dilated layers. The two generations use different defaults, so a result should name the code version (tag or commit), the architecture parameters file and the training data. The trained mouse ESC model from the paper (Oct4, Sox2, Nanog, Klf4) is published on Zenodo and on Kipoi as BPNet-OSKN.

profile.summary: GROVER is a DNA language model pretrained on the human genome. It splits DNA into variable-length tokens learned by byte-pair encoding, and turns a DNA sequence into contextual embeddings. Its authors intend it as a foundation model that is fine-tuned for a specific task, such as promoter identity or protein-DNA binding.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: GROVER is a BERT model for masked language modelling: 12 layers, hidden size 768, 12 attention heads and a vocabulary of 609 tokens. The vocabulary comes from byte-pair encoding of the human genome, and the authors chose the vocabulary size with a next-k-mer prediction task. Because byte-pair tokens depend on the surrounding sequence, a short sequence can be tokenised differently from the same stretch in the whole genome; the card advises adding 100 nucleotides at each end. For a task, the pretrained model is loaded with a classification head and fine-tuned on labelled sequences.

steps.title: Fine-tune on the CTCF example and evaluate
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
import pandas as pd
import wget
import os
import numpy as np

from sklearn.metrics import matthews_corrcoef, accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score, f1_score

import transformers
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, Trainer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification, TrainingArguments
from torch.utils.data import Dataset

CTCF_dataset_url = "https://datashare.tu-dresden.de/s/pjb5gcWGGrbcARN/download/CTCF_dataset.tsv"
file_name = "CTCF_dataset.tsv"
if os.path.exists(file_name):
  os.remove(file_name) # if exists, remove it directly
file_name = wget.download(CTCF_dataset_url, out=file_name)

CTCF_dataset = pd.read_csv('CTCF_dataset.tsv', sep='\t')
train = CTCF_dataset.sample(frac=0.8, random_state=0)
validation = CTCF_dataset.drop(train.index)
test = validation.sample(frac=0.5, random_state=0)
validation = validation.drop(test.index)
train = train.reset_index(drop=True)
validation = validation.reset_index(drop=True)
test = test.reset_index(drop=True)

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("PoetschLab/GROVER")
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained("PoetschLab/GROVER")

class SupervisedDataset(Dataset):
    """Dataset for supervised fine-tuning."""
    def __init__(self, texts, labels, tokenizer):
        super(SupervisedDataset, self).__init__()
        sequences = [text for text in texts]
        output = tokenizer(
            sequences,
            add_special_tokens=True,
            max_length=310,
            padding="longest",
            return_tensors="pt",
            truncation=True
        )
        self.input_ids = output["input_ids"]
        self.attention_mask = output["attention_mask"]
        self.labels = labels
    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.input_ids)
    def __getitem__(self, i):
        return dict(
            input_ids=self.input_ids[i],
            labels=self.labels[i],
            attention_mask=self.attention_mask[i]
        )

train_dataset = SupervisedDataset(train.sequence, train.label, tokenizer)
test_dataset = SupervisedDataset(test.sequence, test.label, tokenizer)
val_dataset = SupervisedDataset(validation.sequence, validation.label, tokenizer)

def calculate_metric_with_sklearn(logits: np.ndarray, labels: np.ndarray):
    predictions = np.argmax(logits, axis=-1)
    return {
        "accuracy": accuracy_score(labels, predictions),
        "f1": f1_score(labels, predictions, average="macro", zero_division=0),
        "matthews_correlation": matthews_corrcoef(labels, predictions),
        "precision": precision_score(labels, predictions, average="macro", zero_division=0),
        "recall": recall_score(labels, predictions, average="macro", zero_division=0),
    }

def compute_metrics(eval_pred):
    logits, labels = eval_pred
    if isinstance(logits, tuple):  # Unpack logits if it's a tuple
        logits = logits[0]
    return calculate_metric_with_sklearn(logits, labels)

train_args = TrainingArguments(seed = 42,
                               output_dir=".",
                               per_device_train_batch_size=16,
                               eval_strategy="epoch",
                               learning_rate=0.000001,
                               num_train_epochs=4
                               )
trainer = transformers.Trainer(
                                model=model,
                                tokenizer=tokenizer,
                                compute_metrics=compute_metrics,
                                train_dataset=train_dataset,
                                eval_dataset=val_dataset,
                                args = train_args
                                )
trainer.train()
results = trainer.evaluate(eval_dataset=test_dataset)
print(results)
PY

profile.summary: RNAErnie is an RNA language model that turns an RNA sequence into embeddings for downstream prediction. During pretraining it uses known RNA motifs as prior knowledge and masks them at random, alongside the usual masked language modelling. Its developers fine-tune it for RNA sequence classification, RNA-RNA interaction prediction and RNA secondary structure prediction.

sections.body: The original RNAErnie is built on the ERNIE model in PaddlePaddle and pretrained with masked language modelling on RNAcentral sequences of up to 512 nucleotides. The released checkpoint combines the BERT, ERNIE and motif masking strategies. Downstream, the developers offer an optional two-stage, type-guided fine-tuning. For RNA secondary structure prediction the repository uses a folding module compiled from mxfold2. The authors' later PyTorch checkpoint is a BERT masked language model with 12 layers, hidden size 768, 12 attention heads and an 11-token vocabulary.

python - <<'PY'
import paddle
from rna_ernie import BatchConverter
from paddlenlp.transformers import ErnieModel

# ========== Set device
paddle.set_device("gpu")

# ========== Prepare Data
data = [
    ("RNA1", "GGGUGCGAUCAUACCAGCACUAAUGCCCUCCUGGGAAGUCCUCGUGUUGCACCCCU"),
    ("RNA2", "GGGUGUCGCUCAGUUGGUAGAGUGCUUGCCUGGCAUGCAAGAAACCUUGGUUCAAUCCCCAGCACUGCA"),
    ("RNA3", "CGAUUCNCGUUCCC--CCGCCUCCA"),
]

# ========== Batch Converter
batch_converter = BatchConverter(k_mer=1,
                                  vocab_path="./data/vocab/vocab_1MER.txt",
                                  batch_size=256,
                                  max_seq_len=512)

# ========== RNAErnie Model
rna_ernie = ErnieModel.from_pretrained("output/BERT,ERNIE,MOTIF,PROMPT/checkpoint_final/")
rna_ernie.eval()

# call batch_converter to convert sequences to batch inputs
for names, _, inputs_ids in batch_converter(data):
    with paddle.no_grad():
        # extract whole sequence embeddings
        embeddings = rna_ernie(inputs_ids)[0].detach()
        # extract [CLS] token embedding
        embeddings_cls = embeddings[:, 0, :]
        print(names, embeddings.shape, embeddings_cls.shape)
PY

profile.summary: RFamLlama is a generative RNA language model conditioned on RNA family. Given an Rfam family ID as a prompt tag, it writes new RNA sequences of that family; the same model can also score sequences for zero-shot fitness prediction. It was trained on sequences from over 4,000 RNA families, each labelled with a family tag.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: RFamLlama is a decoder-only Llama model for causal (next-token) language modelling over a 22-token vocabulary. Each training sequence is preceded by a control tag naming its family. A prompt has the form <|bos|> <|tag_start|> family number <|tag_end|> <|5|>, where the family number is the Rfam ID without the RF prefix; the model then writes the sequence, which ends at the <|3|> token. The developers report that the family tags improve zero-shot fitness prediction; the sources read do not say how a fitness score is computed.

steps.title: Generate sequences for one Rfam family
steps.shell:
python - <<'PY'
# generation
from transformers import LlamaForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, pipeline
import torch
import sys

model_url = "jinyuan22/RFamLlama-base"
model = LlamaForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_url, torch_dtype=torch.float16)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_url)

device = torch.device("cuda:0") if torch.cuda.is_available() else torch.device("cpu")

pipe = pipeline("text-generation", model=model, device=device, tokenizer=tokenizer)

tag = "RF00005"
txt = f"<|bos|> <|tag_start|> {tag[2:]} <|tag_end|> <|5|> "
all_outputs = []
outputs = pipe(txt, num_return_sequences=10, max_new_tokens=300, repetition_penalty=1, top_p=1,temperature=1, do_sample=True)

for i, output in enumerate(outputs):
    seq = output["generated_text"]
    seq = seq.split("<|5|>")[1].split("<|3|>")[0]
    print(f">{i}\n{seq}")
PY

profile.summary: UTR-LM is a language model for the 5' untranslated region (5' UTR) of mRNA, the stretch before the coding sequence that strongly affects how well an mRNA is translated. It reads a 5' UTR sequence and, after fine-tuning, predicts mean ribosome loading, translation efficiency or mRNA expression level. Pretraining combines masked language modelling with labels computed from the sequence, such as secondary structure and minimum free energy.

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: UTR-LM is built on a modified copy of the ESM-2 transformer code, shipped in the repository. The reported settings are 6 transformer layers, 16 attention heads and an embedding size of 128. Pretraining uses masked language modelling (MLM) and, in the recommended variants, also predicts the minimum free energy (MFE) and/or the secondary structure of the sequence. For downstream tasks the developers fine-tune the whole model and feed the [CLS]-token embedding to a predictor trained with Huber loss.

The README's own example pretraining command passes --heads 6 --embed_dim 16, which disagrees with the 16 heads and embedding size 128 listed under General Parameters and in the checkpoint file names. profile.summary: PhyloGPN is a convolutional network that reads DNA sequence alone and outputs, for every position, the parameters of a nucleotide substitution model (Felsenstein's F81). It was trained to fit those parameters to columns of the Zoonomia multispecies whole-genome alignment given a phylogenetic tree, which makes the output a statement about how constrained each site is. It needs no alignment at prediction time, so it can score variants and supply embeddings from a single sequence.
profile.summary_source_locator: docs/models/phylogpn.md opening paragraph; model card first paragraph; arXiv abstract

sections.title: How it works
sections.body: The network is convolutional: 20 stacks of 2 layers with kernel size 5, inner dimension 480 and outer dimension 960, and a receptive field of 481 positions. It is trained to maximise the likelihood of each alignment column under a phylogenetic tree: the output at a position gives the F81 rate parameters for that site, and the stationary distribution of that substitution process says how viable each allele is there. Because the tree and alignment enter only through the loss, prediction takes plain sequence. The model works as a sliding window: an input of length l yields outputs for the l minus 480 central positions, so sequences are padded before scoring.
